events.title: The Peace of Augsburg
events.shortBlurb: The settlement Ferdinand concluded at Augsburg in his brother's name gave Lutheran princes legal standing — and the Empire sixty-three years of peace…
body: After a generation of religious strife, the diet that opened at Augsburg in February 1555 met an absent emperor: Charles V, spent, had left its conduct to his brother Ferdinand, King of the Romans. On 25 September the peace was published in the emperor's name with the princes of the Augsburg Confession.

Its rule was cuius regio, eius religio: the prince's faith, Catholic or the Lutheranism of Augsburg, should be the faith of his territory, the dissenter free to sell his goods and depart. At Ferdinand's insistence the reservatum ecclesiasticum guarded the lands of any prince-bishop who should turn Protestant, a clause the Protestant estates never accepted; Calvinism and the sects stood outside the peace altogether.

Within weeks Charles resigned the Netherlands and Spain, and the imperial crown followed. The settlement the old emperor had shunned to sign held the German peace for sixty-three years — until a defenestration at Prague in 1618 opened the Thirty Years' War and taught Europe how much the peace of Augsburg had left undone.
